_meta.source: JRC ASAP (Anomaly hot Spots of Agricultural Production)
_meta.notes: Current-season agricultural stress from the EC Joint Research Centre's ASAP monthly expert assessment. Latest assessment per country from the full 2016-present series; most recent date in this run 2026-07-11. hotspot_code: 0 no hotspot, 1 hotspot, 2 major hotspot. ASAP's raw hs_code 3 means NOT ASSESSED, not a severity above 2 — those countries (8 in this run) carry hotspot_code null and stress_score null. NULL IS NOT ZERO: no assessment is not an all-clear, and several unassessed countries have dozens of subnational crop warnings standing (units_crop_warning is populated regardless of code). stress_score 0-100 is banded by the JRC verdict (0-20 / 40-70 / 75-100 for codes 0/1/2) and spread within band by units_crop_warning normalised against that country's own historical maximum — so the expert verdict always dominates the ranking and the count only breaks ties. COVERAGE IS NOT GLOBAL: ASAP monitors 81 food-insecure countries only. A country absent from this payload is one ASAP does not watch (USA, Ukraine, Brazil, India, Australia among them) — absence must NOT be presented as an absence of stress. Unlike Aqueduct baseline and CCKP normals, this is a current-season signal and goes stale monthly; ASAP publishes around the 10th.

KGZ.comment: In Kyrgyzstan, harvest of winter wheat is underway with good prospects thanks to above average crop biomass in all regions, while spring wheat, to be harvested as from September is in good conditions. After a drier than average start to the season in October and especially November, moisture conditions have been conducive for cereals growth with abundant rainfall in December followed by close to average rainfall from January to June, except for a dry spell from mid March to mid April.

BGD.comment: In Bangladesh, prospects are favourable for Aman rice (35% of the country total rice production) in vegetative to reproductive stage and Aus rice (10% of the country total rice production) whose harvest is underway as crop biomass is above average thanks to abundant rainfall, that also resulted in floods and landslides affecting more than 1 million people according to [https://www.iom.int/news/heavy-monsoon-rains-hit-over-1m-bangladesh-iom-scales-emergency-response] IOM press release of 16 July 2026.

TJK.comment: In Tajikistan, harvest of winter and spring wheat is underway with very good prospects thanks to well above average crop biomass. After a drier than average start to the season in October November, good rainfall in December and early February and up to 8C above average temperatures in February boosted cereals growth, hence the very good prospects for this ongoing harvest.

SDN.comment:
The early season rainfall deficits described in June have worsened in July, where below average rainfall and high temperatures prevailed across the main agricultural seasons in Northern Kordofan, North and West Darfur, White and Blue Nile. Across these regions a strong negative biomass anomaly is visible at the end of July. 
Seasonal forecasts from ICPAC and the Copernicus multi-model ensemble for the rest of the July-September rainy season indicate a high probability of below-average rainfall largely driven by ongoing El Niño conditions. This is further supported by ASAP seasonal forecast warnings, highlighting an elevated risk of below-average rainfall across all agricultural and pastoral areas of the country. The delayed start of the season increases concerns about low areas planted and early season crop failure as well as rapid decrease of pastoral vegetation availability. The main seasons of 2024 and 2025 have been characterized by generally favourable rainfall conditions. Although positive agroclimatic conditions alone were clearly not sufficient to restore rural livelihoods, they have still been supporting local crop and livestock production activities under difficult security conditions and with limited access to farming inputs. 
On the contrary, the 2026 dry conditions, if they continue as predicted through the main season as predicted, will further worsen large-scale population displacement and compound the widespread destruction of agricultural assets, infrastructure, and basic services. After more than three years of conflict Sudan is one of the gravest food and nutrition crises globally, with 19,5 Million people affected by high levels of acute food insecurity and several areas at risk of famine as confirmed by IPC in May 2026. The [https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Sudan_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Feb2026_Jan2027_Special_Snapshot.pdf] IPC partial coverage special snapshot update for June–September 2026, covering 56 of Sudan's 195 localities and IDP settlements, identified a risk of famine in 14 areas across North Darfur, South Darfur, and South Kordofan under a reasonable worst-case scenario. The lean season is expected to continue until late 2026, while food prices are rising rapidly, further exacerbated by disruptions to global markets linked to the conflict involving Iran.

MOZ.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country and regional performance varies due to flooding and dry spells that triggered widespread crop failures during critical stages of plant development. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-humanitarian-snapshot-may-2026-enpt] OCHA, "nationwide, more than 518,000 hectares of cultivated land were affected, including 312,000 hectares destroyed, with the most severe impacts recorded in Gaza, Maputo, and Sofala provinces where crop losses exceeded 50% in some areas". Moreover, northern Mozambique faces Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity through January 2027 despite the current harvest ([https://fews.net/southern-africa/mozambique/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWS NET, June 2026). According to [https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] FAO, Crop Prospects and Food Situation (July 2026), the national harvest is estimated to be close to the five‑year average. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across most parts of the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

CUB.comment: In July, the main cycles of maize, rice, and sweet potatoes should be in the sowing stage. The island is facing a severe and unprecedented national emergency due to the oil embargo and tightened sanctions, accompanied by national electric grid collapses ([https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/cubas-national-electric-grid-collapses-third-time-july-state-media-says-2026-07-14/] Reuters). The agricultural sector is severely affected, with harvests rotting in the fields and farmers selling their land due to the inability to plant, irrigate, or move goods to market ([https://www.ft.com/content/859ff727-3a8b-42df-a6d8-7d55ed0e8264?syn-25a6b1a6=1] Financial Times).

LAO.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

DJI.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

UZB.comment: In Uzbekistan, harvest of winter cereals is underway with very good prospects as crop biomass is the highest since 2002 across all regions. After a drier than average start to the season in October and November, rainfall conditions improved and together with above average temperatures (of up to 9C in February) boosted crop growth.

MDG.comment: In Madagascar, harvest of rice and maize in the northern and central areas finalized in June with an overall output estimated close to average due to mixed crop conditions: above average crop biomass in Alaotra Mangoro, close to average in Vakinankaratra, Itasy and Analamanga, slightly below average in Sofia (possibly due to cyclone Fitya at end of January). The rice season started in November with good rainfall till December-January, then rainfall conditions shifted to below average levels in February in the centre north (from Analamanga to Sofia and Diana) and particularly in March in the central Highlands (from Haute Matsiatra to Alaotra Mangoro), and to a lower extent in April in Vakinankaratra and Bongolava in the central highlands, at the start of harvest.In the Grand South, below average rainfall since early February, combined with about 2C above average temperatures from February to May accelerated crop senescence and resulted in below average output of cereals and legume crops, especially in Anosy and Androy. The region is projected to have about 1.5 to 2.0 million people in acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 and above) as a result of previous droughts (2020, 2021 and 2022), cyclones, poor socio economic conditions and aid reduction, according to the latest [https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1161004/?iso3=MDG] IPC analysis and [https://reliefweb.int/report/madagascar/madagascar-food-security-outlook-early-lean-season-and-el-nino-challenge-food-security-grand-south-june-2026-january-2027] FEWS-NET.

SLV.comment: In July, the primera cycle of maize and beans as well as the main cycle of rice should be in the vegetation stage, while the sorghum cycle in the late sowing stage.The season started with irregular, below-average rainfall which likely induced smallholder households to delay planting. In the past month, rainfall has been below average, reaching over 50% lower levels in the Eastern region. Vegetation conditions are poor in most cropping areas, particularly across 67% of the Eastern region, suggesting negative prospects for the crops development. According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S multi-model, there is a high probability of very drier-than-normal conditions throughout the rest of the year.

MLI.comment: Planting of coarse grain crops (maize, millet, and sorghum) is almost finished in the southern part of the country, whereas rice planting is ongoing in northern parts of the country. A delay in crop growth is visible in the Ségou, Koulikoro, and Sikasso regions, where approximately 45% to 65% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. Crop conditions are affected to a lesser extent in the regions of Mopti and Kayes, where roughly 30% to 35% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. Similarly, rangeland conditions in some of the southern agricultural zones (Koulikoro, Ségou) and parts of the northern regions (Tomboctou, Gao) are below-average. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the August–September 2026 period points to drier-than-average conditions across the country's southern agropastoral zones. Consequently, [https://fews.net/west-africa/mali/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWSNET (June 2026) projects that agricultural production and localized cereal yields will decline across southern, western, and conflict-affected regions, driven by poor seasonal rainfall forecasts, restricted access to farming inputs, and ongoing insecurity that triggers displacement and prevents farmers from reaching their fields.

CAF.comment: Rice and cassava are currently in the growth stage, while mixed precipitation performances have characterized the last three dekads. Below-average rainfall has been recorded in the west (Ouham Pendé, -21%), while in contrast above average levels hit the east (Basse-Kotto, +24%). According to the latest [https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] Crop Prospects and Food Situation report, about 2 million people (approximately 33 percent of the total population) are estimated to be facing acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between April and August 2026, driven by ongoing conflict and constrained agricultural production.

GHA.comment: In the southern part of the country, the main season maize harvest will begin in August. Cumulative rainfall over the past three months shows notable variations across the country, with deficits impacting the Northern and Brong Ahafo regions, near-average conditions in the far north, and above-average rainfall across the southern coastal zone. Crop conditions in mid-July are close to average in the south, pointing to an average output. In contrast, rice, sorghum, and millet crops in the northern part of the country are currently in the growing stage, where conditions in the Northern, Upper West, and Upper East regions remain below-average due to a negative greenness anomaly affecting approximately 25% to 40% of the active crop area. Meanwhile, pasture biomass conditions in the main grazing areas of the north and center remain average to slightly above-average. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 points to average rainfall conditions across most of the country, except for the southwest where drier-than-average conditions are forecast. These dry projections follow the events of June 29, 2026, when torrential rains triggered devastating floods across Ghana's southern coastline—specifically impacting the Greater Accra, Central, and Western regions—which paralyzed economic activity, submerged properties, killed at least 12 people, and forced the emergency evacuation of hundreds of stranded residents ([https://reliefweb.int/report/ghana/gha-flood-06-2026-floods-2026-06-30] IFRC).

AFG.comment:
In Afghanistan, harvest finalized in July for winter wheat and is ongoing for spring cereals with good prospects for both types of crops thanks to average to above average crop biomass. The winter cereals season started with poor rainfall in November, but rainfall conditions improved in the following months resulting in good biomass for winter and spring cereals as well as for (irrigated) summer crops (rice planted in May-June and maize sown in May). The ongoing dry season, which started in June, will end in September and rainfall is forecast above average for the October-December period (as a result of El Nino), which should support sowings of winter cereals.
 Afghanistan continues to face high levels of hunger with about 14 million people estimated in acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 or above) for the period April – September 2026 as a result of prolonged economic deterioration, recurrent drought, refugee returns, declining humanitarian aid and decreasing remittances according to the latest [https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Afghanistan_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Sept2025_Sept2026_Report.pdf] IPC report from 16 December 2025 and [https://www.wfp.org/emergencies/afghanistan] WFP.

HTI.comment: In July, the main cycle of maize should normally be in the harvesting stage, while the minor cycle of rice and maize and the cycle of sorghum are in the sowing stage. Rainfall in the past month has been below normal in most part of the country, potentially hindering the correct establishment of minor cycle crops. Vegetation conditions are normal to good in most cropping areas, however, the spread of insecurity to key agricultural areas, in particular the key department of Artibonite, and trade corridors continues to disrupt livelihoods, markets, and trade flows. According to the ([https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel), there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the entire country through the remainder of 2026.

TZA.comment: Harvest is underway for Msimu crops in unimodal areas (sorghum, rice, and maize) and Masika crops in bimodal areas (sorghum, millet, and maize). Precipitation has been recorded in average during the last 30 days. Biomass is now in average throughout the country with the exception of Morogoro, Pwani and Tanga, which suffer from previous lack of rainfall. In Dodoma, the country's top cereal-producing region, biomass is recorded above average (+10%). According to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=TZA] FAO/GIEWS, aggregate cereal production in 2026 is tentatively forecast at near-average levels of 12.8 million tonnes, despite localized production shortfalls caused by erratic seasonal rains and prolonged dry spells, compounded by low fertilizer application rates linked to post-election port disruptions and rising international input prices; about 507,000 people (5 percent of the analysed population) are projected to face severe acute food insecurity between June 2026 and January 2027. [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service point to dry outlook until September, particuralrly in the north, followed by a sudden shift to wet from October, in agreement with the expected influence of ongoing El Niño conditions.

BWA.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country, and the cereal output is expected to be above the five-year average ([https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] FAO, Crop Prospects and Food Situation (July 2026)). Additionally, the favourable weather has significantly improved rangelands, which is set to boost livestock production. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

IRQ.comment: In Iraq, harvest of winter cereals finalized in June with favourable prospects in all governorates except the southern ones (Babil, Qadissiya, Wassit, Thi-Qar, Missan) where the government limited surface irrigation to 50% of the usual area. After a drier than average start to the season in October-November, rainfall improved as from December and remained average to above average across the country, which favoured cereals growth and resulted in above average cereals biomass in the main producing areas of the north. In contrast, in the south, cereals biomass is well below average except in Najaf, for which winter cereals benefited from modern irrigation fostered by the government. Overall, at country level, output is expected to be above average. This year, in contrast with 2025, 2023 and 2022, rice cultivation has been authorized in the south (Najaf, Qadissiya) and rice planting took place from mid June to mid July (see flooded rice fields in Qadissiya at end July 2026 on [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/06804797] S2 imagery).

EGY.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

NER.comment: The planting of cereal crops (millet, sorghum, and rice) is ongoing across the country under average rainfall conditions, except for southeastern Niger, where a rainfall deficit was observed over the last month (approximately 30%–35% below-average cumulative rainfall). As a result, a delay in the start of the cropping season has been observed in the regions of Maradi, Tahoua, and Diffa. Similarly, a delay in the growth of rangeland biomass has been noted in the regions of Zinder, Diffa, and Maradi. However, there is still time for improvement at this stage of the season, making close monitoring of the situation over the coming weeks crucial. Meanwhile, ongoing insecurity persists in the Tillabéry and Diffa regions, as well as in the northwestern part of Tahoua. This insecurity restricts access to fields and markets, disrupts livelihoods, and leads to poor harvests and severe food consumption deficits (IPC Phase 3 and 4) through January 2027 ([https://fews.net/fr/west-africa/niger/perspectives-sur-la-securite-alimentaire/juin-2026] FEWSNET, June 2026). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 indicates continued below-average rainfall in the southeast, despite average conditions elsewhere.

MMR.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

SEN.comment: Despite it being early in the agricultural cycle with time for potential recovery, a significant dry spell, with rainfall tracking 40% to 60% below-average, has delayed the start of the cropping season and also delayed rangeland biomass growth across all northern and central-western regions. While the planting of coarse grains (maize, millet, and sorghum) is expected to be finalized by the end of July, rice cultivation will continue until the end of August. Compounding these current deficits, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 points to drier-than-average conditions across the entire country.

ECU.comment: In July, the main cycle of maize concluded the harvesting stage, while the minor cycle completed the vegetation stage. The minor rice cycle typically completes the sowing stage during this time.Vegetation conditions are average to above average in most cropping areas suggesting good harvest prospects for the main cycle of maize. Cumulative rainfall in the past three months has been average to below average in the eastern part of the country.According to the ([https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel), there is a very high probability that conditions will be wetter than normal in the coastal areas and normal to drier than normal in the northern and western part of the country through the end of the year. In July, the Comité Nacional para el Estudio Regional del Fenómeno El Niño (CN-ERFEN) updated its status from "El Niño Under Observation" to "El Niño Active" and recommended that the National Secretariat for Risk Management establish an Orange Alert ([https://www.inocar.mil.ec/web/index.php/boletines/erfen] ERFEN).

SSD.comment:
After abundant rainfall at the beginning of the season, showers have been more irregular through May, June and July across most parts of the country. Despite this recent rainfall deficit, overall vegetation conditions remain generally above average, reflecting the normal rainfall received earlier in the season since March. 
Seasonal forecasts from the ICPAC and Copernicus for the July–September period indicate a high likelihood of below-average rainfall, primarily associated with ongoing El Niño conditions. Also, independently from agro-climatic conditions, both farmers and pastoralists are highly vulnerable to the impact of conflict, economic downturn, high influx of refugees from Kordofan and internally displaced population. This scenario is further worsened by the economic effects of the conflict in Iran. An estimated 7.8 million people are experiencing IPC Phase 3 or higher (Crisis or worse) according to IPC projection update for the period from April to July 2026. This includes approximately 73,000 in IPC phase 5 (catastrophe), 2.5 million people in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) and 5.3 million in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis). According to the update, conditions have sharply worsened, with a risk of famine now identified in Luakpiny/Nasir, Ulang, Nyirol, and Akobo, driven by conflict, displacement, and restricted aid access.

MRT.comment: Planting of coarse grains (maize, millet and sorghum) is ongoing, whilst planting of irrigated rice that is the major cereal produced in the country, is almost completed. A severe moisture deficit is evident across Mauritania's primary agricultural and agropastoral belts, with the most pronounced negative precipitation anomalies concentrated throughout Trarza, Brakna, Gorgol, Guidimakha, and Assaba (ca.40%-70% below-average cumulative rainfall in the last month). As a result, a delay in the start of the cropping season is observed, as well as a delay in the growth of rangeland biomass. There is still time for improvement at this stage of the season and monitoring of the situation in the next weeks is crucial. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 points to drier-than-average conditions across the southern tip and southwestern agricultural border regions of Mauritania. According to the latest [https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] FAO, Crop Prospects and Food Situation (July 2026) report, as of early May 2026, a steady influx of Malian conflict refugees pushed the registered displaced population to 184,000, with 90% concentrated in the resource-scarce Hodh Ech Chargui region.

AGO.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country and agricultural production is likely to be below average at the national level due to a very dry and poorly distributed October to May rainy season. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across many coastal and southern parts of the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

NIC.comment: In July, highland rice, sorghum, and the primera cycle of maize are in the vegetation stage, while the harvest of the primera bean cycle begins. Rainfall during the past three months has been over a third below average, resulting in delayed planting and poor vegetation conditions across more than 40% of the country. Central and coastal departments are the most severely affected. According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=north_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel, the situation will remain dire as there is a high probability of very dry conditions through the rest of the year across the entire country.

ERI.comment: Crop areas in Gash Barka and Debub have experienced heat and rainfall deficits up to 30% in the last 90 days. Similar conditions affect also rangeland areas in the north east of the country. ASAP forecast warnings predict negative vegetation anomalies for the rest of the main season.

HND.comment: In June, the primera cycle of maize and beans should be normally in the vegetation stage, while the sorghum cycle is in the sowing stage. Rainfall in the past three months has been almost 50% below average and vegetation conditions appear very poor, especially in the departments of Choluteca, Comayagua, Olancho and Cortes, which are key maize-producing areas. This is also due to the reduced planted area following the erratic start of the season and the soaring prices of agricultural inputs and fertilisers for the primera seasons crops ([https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=HND" target="_blank] FAO GIEWS). For the period between April to July 2026, it is the IPC projects that around 1.8 million people (18% of the population) could be facing a Food Crisis or Emergency situation (IPC Phase 3 or 4) ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1163882/?iso3=HND] IPC).

DZA.comment: In Algeria, harvest of wheat and barley finalized with very good prospects after three to five years of below average output in the western part of the country. [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country/DZA/pdf/DZA.pdf] FAO GIEWS forecasts wheat and barley productions at 3.5 and 1.3 million tons, i.e. 28 and 40% above their 5 year average respectively, making it the highest harvest since 2019, while [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC145926] JRC MARS bulletin of June 2026 estimates wheat and barley yields at +17% and +55% above their five-year average respectively. The winter cereals season started with mixed conditions, i.e. low rainfall in the western half of the country that delayed winter cereals growth while closer to average moisture conditions in the eastern half of the country resulted in average to above average crop biomass. As from December, rainfall improved and fostered cereals growth across the country, including in the western part, resulting in well above average biomass across the country. Prospects are hence very good, despite however above average temperatures since June across the country, and especially in the west, that are likely to reduce yields due to a shortened grain filling period.

BOL.comment: In July, wheat, sorghum, and minor-season maize entered the harvesting stage. The eastern part of the country is off-season. Rainfall has been above average over the past three months, and vegetation conditions in Santa Cruz, the main cereal-producing area, remain good. However, since April, Bolivia has experienced nationwide fuel and foreign currency reserve shortages, constraining machinery operations and input availability. In an attempt to restore economic stability, the country will end a 15-year U.S. dollar peg by the end of this month ([https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/bolivia-ends-15-year-dollar-peg-attempt-restore-economic-stability-2026-06-27/] Reuters). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel, there is a high probability of wetter than normal conditions persisting through September in the central and northern part of the country.

ZMB.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country and according to the [https://www.agriculture.gov.zm/2026/05/zambia-projected-to-produce-nearly-5-million-metric-tonnes-of-maize/] Ministry of Agriculture of Zambia, the maize harvest is projected at 4,937,605 metric tonnes, making it the highest maize production ever recorded in the country’s history. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across southern and southwestern Zambia for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

CIV.comment: Across the southern and central bimodal areas of the country, cumulative rainfall from the start of the rainy season in March until mid-July has been average to above-average, benefiting crop and rangeland conditions. Harvesting operations in the center and south are expected to begin in August, and a good output is anticipated. In the northern unimodal areas, the planting of coarse grain and rice crops was finalized in July. Below-average crop conditions are observed in the northern districts of Savanes and Denguélé, where around 30% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast  for the August–September 2026 period points to average rainfall conditions across the country. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/cote-divoire/unicef-cote-divoire-humanitarian-situation-report-no-2-1-april-30-june-2026] UNICEF, the deteriorating security crisis in Mali and Burkina Faso has driven approximately 85,630 refugees and asylum seekers (as of mid-May)—nearly 50,000 of whom are children—to seek safety in northern Côte d’Ivoire.

GTM.comment: In July, the primera cycle of maize and beans as well as the main cycle of rice should be in the vegetation stage. However, as the start of the season was marked by below average in nearly all cropping areas, planting has likely been delayed. Rainfall was below average also in the past month, resulting in poor vegetation conditions, especially in Verapaz, Central Area and Motagua Valley. According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel, there is a high probability of much drier-than-normal conditions through the end of the year.

TGO.comment: In the southern bimodal areas, main-season maize harvesting will begin in August with an anticipated average yield. The sowing of millet and sorghum concludes in late July and rice is in the growing stage. Below-average vegetation conditions are observed in the northern regions of Savanes and Kara. A greenness anomaly affects roughly 40% to 50% of the active crop area and 35% to 40% of active rangelands in the two regions. These poor crop conditions stem from severe early-season dry spells—with rainfall tracking 60% to 70% below average in April, and 20% to 25% below average from late June to mid-July—compounded by escalating localized conflict. Driven by armed group incursions and a state of security emergency along the northern borders, the spillover effects of the Sahel crisis will continue to degrade livelihoods, displace populations, and disrupt socio-economic activities in Savanes, particularly within the Kpendjal and Kpendjal-Ouest prefectures ([https://fews.net/fr/west-africa/togo/perspectives-sur-la-securite-alimentaire/juin-2026] FEWSNET, June 2026). Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 points to average rainfall conditions across the country.

MAR.comment: In Morocco, after 4 years of below average production due to low rainfall, harvest of winter wheat and barley finalized in June with very favourable prospects: with respect to their last five-year average, yields of wheat and barley are forecast to increase by 37% and 51% respectively according to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC145926] JRC MARS bulletin from June while [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country/MAR/pdf/MAR.pdf] FAO GIEWS forecasts wheat and barley productions at +23 and -7% respectively in early July (the close to average barley production forecast is possibly due to a reduction in the sown area). The 2025-2026 season started badly with drier than average conditions from October to mid November; however rainfall improved at end November and especially in December and January in the whole country and in February in the north, reaching in mid June the best total rainfall for the winter crop season of the last 25 years in the centre-west of the country, from Tadla Azizal and Chaouia to Gharb, i.e. the main cereals producing regions. As a result of this very good rainfall, winter crops reached well above average biomass levels in all provinces, including in the eastern regions (Tadla Azilal, Meknes and Oriental) where cereals growth was initially strongly delayed. This very good rainfall also resulted in prolonged flooding in February in Gharb and localized areas of Tanger Tetouan, which damaged crops due to the persistence of water; however at country level, this production loss is negligible.

TUN.comment: In Tunisia, harvest of winter barley and wheat finalized in June with favourable prospects due to well above average crop biomass across all governorates. According to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC145926] JRC MARS bulletin from June, wheat and barley yields are forecast at 15% and 26% above their respective last five year average. The season started badly in the eastern half of the country with rainfall deficit in October and November which resulted in delayed cereals growth in Zaghouan, Ben Arous, and Nabeul; however moisture conditions improved in the following months and fostered winter crops development, resulting in above average crop biomass in all governorates.

TKM.comment: In Turkmenistan, harvest of winter cereals is underway with very good prospects as crop biomass is well above average in all regions supported by average to above average rainfall since December and average to above average temperatures since October, in particular in February where temperatures reached 8C above normal.

PHL.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

IRN.comment: In Iran, harvest of winter wheat finalized in July across the country with average to above average prospects in all provinces except in the centre (Tehran, Markazi, Esfahan, Ghazvin), where crop biomass is below average. After a drier than average start to the season in October and especially November, moisture conditions improved across the country with average to abundant rainfall from December to May, causing even flooding at end March during the conflict with US and Israel (see [https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/iran-islamic-republic/islamic-republic-iran-humanitarian-update-no-02-3-april-2026] OCHA report). This good rainfall supported crop growth and resulted in average to above average biomass of winter cereals in all provinces, including the centre west (Kordestan, Kermanshah, Lorestan, Hamedan) where crop growth was delayed; the only exception is an area in the centre between Tehran and Esfahan where crop biomass is below average. Overall, at country level, winter cereals output is expected above average. In northern Iran (Gilan, Mazandaran and Golestan), rice is growing under favourable conditions.

NAM.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country, and the cereal output is expected to be above the five-year average ([https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] FAO, Crop Prospects and Food Situation (July 2026)). According to preliminary data from the Namibian Agronomic Board the white maize production is forecast at 111,447 tonnes, representing a significant 37% increase compared to last year's harvest ([https://www.nbcnews.na/node/116305] NBC News). Additionally, the favourable weather has significantly improved rangelands, which is set to boost livestock production. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across many parts of country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

GMB.comment: The planting of maize, for harvest in September, and rice, millet, and sorghum for harvest in October, is nearly complete. However, rainfall was well below average between mid-June and the beginning of July, with cumulative rainfall dropping to 60% below average for this period. As a result, a slight delay in the start of the cropping season has been observed. While it is still early in the season and there is room for improvement, close monitoring over the coming weeks remains crucial. Meanwhile, pastoral biomass conditions currently stand at an average level. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 points to drier-than-average conditions across the country.

KHM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

LSO.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country, with a varying regional performance: favourable rains benefitted crop development in the Northern Lowlands and Foothills leading to an above-average harvest, while late-season flooding caused widespread crop damage and below-average yields in the Southern Lowlands and Senqu River Valley ([https://fews.net/southern-africa/lesotho/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWSNET, June 2026). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

VNM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

CMR.comment: In the northern unimodal rainfall areas, the planting of 2026 millet and sorghum crops was completed by June, with harvesting expected to begin in late September; meanwhile, the main maize harvest will start mid-August in central and southern regions. While generally beneficial agroclimatic conditions have supported crop and pasture development in the south, conditions remain below average in the Nord and Extrême-Nord regions, where approximately 35% to 40% of the active crop area is affected by negative greenness anomalies. However, because it is still early in the agricultural season, remains room for potential improvement in these areas. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast  for August–September 2026 points to wetter-than-average conditions across most parts of the country, except for the Far North region, where drier-than-average conditions are forecast to persist. According to [https://fews.net/west-africa/cameroon/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWS NET (June 2026), protracted conflict and escalating insurgent attacks across northern and western Cameroon continue to drive widespread displacement, restrict farmland access, and disrupt vital agropastoral livelihoods, sustaining Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity through January 2027. Furthermore, the [https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] FAO, Crop Prospects and Food Situation (July 2026) report highlights that “elevated fuel prices continued to increase transport costs, putting upward pressure on prices of food and agricultural inputs”.

LKA.comment: In Sri Lanka, prospects for second season (Yala) rice and maize to be harvested as from August are good thanks to above average crop biomass in the main producing provinces.

ZAF.comment: The main cereal season has concluded in the country. According to the [https://www.sagis.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/CEC_2026-07-28.pdf] Crop Estimates Committee (CEC)’s sixth production forecast, total maize output is estimated at 17,362 million tonnes, standing more than 10% above the 5-year average. In the Western Cape, winter cereal biomass conditions are well above-average. However, the [https://www.sagis.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/CEC_2026-07-28.pdf] preliminary area planted to wheat is approximately 10% below-average the 5-year average. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across most of the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These projections align with expectations surrounding the upcoming El Niño event and will require close monitoring over the coming months.

COG.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

MWI.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country, with average yields according to [https://fews.net/southern-africa/malawi/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWS NET (June 2026), however, dry spells and flooding caused below-average harvests in southern livelihood zones (Southern Lakeshore, Middle Shire, and Lower Shire).

BDI.comment: Harvest of season B crops is complete for beans and ongoing for sorghum and maize, while the country experienced in-average rainfall during the last 30 days. Below average biomass areas are recorded particularly in the west and in the north. In Bujumbura, 36% of the active cropland is in poor vegetation status. Despite pockets of below-average biomass, Gitega, which accounts for 11.7% of national cereal production, showed average biomass conditions throughout Season B. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/burundi/rapport-d-valuation-des-recoltes-des-approvisionnements-alimentaires-pour-la-saison] FEWSNET, the 2026B harvest will be cumulatively below-average in the semi-arid regions of the country (Imbo Plains, Northern Lowlands, and Eastern Lowlands), but cumulatively near-average nationally due to tubers and perennial crops balancing out large losses of beans.

NGA.comment: Below-average cumulative rainfall was observed across most of Nigeria last month, particularly impacting the Middle Belt and southern coastal regions, while localized average to above-average conditions were limited to parts of the northeast and southwest. Consequently, poor crop and pastoral conditions are severely affecting the country's main agricultural zones. In the Middle Belt states of Niger and Plateau, negative greenness anomalies affect around 45% to 65% of the active crop area. A similar trend is visible across the North-West zone, where 35% to 65% of the farming areas in Kaduna, Jigawa, and Kano are impacted, while 25% to 40% of the active crop area in the North-East states is similarly affected. These poor agricultural conditions might be attributed to the ongoing insecurity and economic hardships. According to [https://fews.net/west-africa/nigeria/integrated-food-security-analysis/june-2026] FEWSNET (June 2026), escalating conflict across northern Nigeria is severely disrupting the 2026 agricultural season by restricting farmland access and forcing illegal harvest taxes. Furthermore, high fuel and fertilizer prices are already driving reductions in total planted area nationwide ([https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] FAO, Crop Prospects and Food Situation, July 2026). Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast  for the August–September 2026 period points to average conditions across most parts of the country, except for the northeastern region where drier-than-average conditions are expected to persist. As a result, the humanitarian outlook is critical. The latest Cadre Harmonisé update indicates that a sharp increase from October projections will leave 36.3 million people in Nigeria facing Crisis or worse food insecurity (CH Phase 3+) during the peak of the 2026 lean season from June to August ([https://reliefweb.int/report/nigeria/wfp-nigeria-country-brief-june-2026] WFP Nigeria Country Brief, June 2026). North-East Nigeria is experiencing its worst food crisis in over a decade, with 36% of the population—approximately 6.4 million people—projected to encounter Crisis or worse outcomes. This figure includes more than 1.1 million people facing Emergency (CH Phase 4) conditions and 10,300 facing Catastrophe (CH Phase 5) ([https://fscluster.org/sites/default/files/2026-07/NE%20Nigeria%20Food%20Security%20Season%20Lean%20Season%20Advocacy%20Note%20June%202026.pdf] Food Security Sector Nigeria, 2026. Nigeria Food Security Season Lean Season Advocacy Note June 2026. Food Security Cluster).

SOM.comment:
The 2026 Gu season in Somalia has been characterized by a delayed onset, erratic rainfall distribution and high temperatures, causing drought conditions in parts of the south and central parts of the country since May 2026. Vegetation conditions observed in late July indicate that drought conditions have caused crop failure in rainfed areas across parts of Bay, Juba and Shabelle regions and low rangelands productivity in the same regions as well as extending further to parts of central Somalia and Puntland. 
At harvesting time, there are high concerns that a partial 2026 Gu harvest failure will compound the severe impacts of the 2025 Deyr drought, during which large parts of the country experienced crop failure or significantly below-average yields, alongside reduced livestock production. According to [https://fews.net/east-africa/somalia] FEWSNET, there is a credible risk of famine in parts of Bay Region due to the delayed onset and poor performance of the 2026 Gu rains following consecutive drought seasons. At the same time, Somalia remains highly dependent on imported food and fuel from the Gulf region, leaving it vulnerable to regional supply disruptions and price shocks.

COD.comment: The second season maize, rice (north), cassava (south), and yams are being harvested, while maize (center/main) and cassava (south) are beginning to be planted. Average to slightly below average precipitation has been recorded throughout the country in the last 30 days. In Ituri, biomass indicators are below average (-9%), in consequence of the erratic precipitation received in the last 3 months. According to the latest [https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] Crop Prospects and Food Situation report, harvesting of main season maize is expected to commence in November, while the ongoing conflict, intensified since January 2025 in eastern regions, has led to widespread displacement and restricted access to agricultural fields keeping the cereal planted area at a below-average level.

LBR.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

PRK.comment: In DPRK, rice and maize are in vegetative growth under favourable rainfall conditions and crop biomass is above average across all provinces.

KEN.comment: Vegetation conditions across much of Kenya deteriorated compared to June, reflecting the cumulative effects of below-average rainfall since late May and throughout June and July. The resulting moisture deficits are likely to have adversely affected pasture resources, particularly in the arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs). In the unimodal cropping zones, below-average rainfall slowed crop development and reduced soil moisture availability during critical crop growth stages. The impacts of the prolonged dry conditions are already evident across parts of western Kenya, including Kakamega, Bungoma, Uasin Gishu, Elgeyo Marakwet, and Trans Nzoia counties, among others. In several of the North Rift cereal-producing areas, prolonged moisture stress has resulted in irreversible crop wilting, with some maize fields unlikely to recover before harvest. [https://nation.africa/kenya/news/erratic-weather-puts-kenya-s-breadbasket-on-edge-5497196#story] Media reports and official government statements indicate that the prolonged July dry spell is already affecting crop production in several of Kenya's major cereal-producing counties with localized yield losses estimated at up to 60%. Looking ahead, forecasts of a strong El Niño for the upcoming short rains season point to an increased risk of adverse impacts including increased risk of flooding and other weather-related hazards. These conditions could further affect agricultural production, disrupt livelihoods, and complicate recovery efforts in areas already impacted by the current dry spell.

YEM.comment: In Yemen, in the Central Highlands and Southern Uplands, sorghum and millet in early vegetative growth received half of the usual rainfall in the last month, while sowings of main sorghum and millet are ongoing in the Coastal Areas under slightly below average moisture conditions. Drier than average conditions are forecast to continue in August and September, which constitute the main part of the sorghum season, after which rainfall is forecast above average for the end of season. Food insecurity remains high with about 17 million food insecure people out of 40 million people according to [https://www.wfp.org/countries/yemen] WFP, mainly as a result of the socio economic conditions and conflict.

TLS.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

SLE.comment: The planting of minor coarse grains (sorghum, millet, and maize) began in May and concluded in June for sorghum and in July for millet and maize. Meanwhile, the planting of rice, the country's primary cereal crop, is underway and expected to wrap up by the end of July. Cumulative rainfall across the Northern and Southern provinces has been highly erratic; it was poor in May (approximately 50% to 65% below-average), recovered from early to mid-June, but dropped significantly below average again from late June to mid-July (approximately 35% to 50% below average). Consequently, water-stressed vegetation conditions are now visible in both provinces. In contrast, while the Eastern province also faced a poor start in May (approximately 30% below average), above-average rainfall since early June has successfully supported crop development. Despite these mixed crop conditions, pastoral biomass as of mid-July remains at an average to slightly above-average level nationwide. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 points to average rainfall conditions across the country.

LBY.comment: In Libya, harvest of barley and wheat finalized in May and June respectively with mixed prospects, i.e. poor in the Tripoli area going from Az Zawia to Misurata, most likely due to a reduction of the sown area, and good around Banghazi (e.g. in Al Fatah) except in Darnah, where crop biomass is well below average, probably due to a reduction in the sown area.

RWA.comment: Season B harvest is complete for beans and ongoing for sorghum and maize. While precipitation has been recorded in-average during the last 30 days, biomass indicators are below average particularly [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6bbac73] in the east of the country. In Kirehe, accounting for the 7% of the national cereal production, 42% of the active cropland is seen in poor vegetation status. ASAP end of season biomass warnings are present in 13 districts. The latest [https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] Crop Prospects and Food Situation report confirms that, in Rwanda, uneven seasonal rainfall patterns are expected to constrain yields of the 2026B harvests. [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service point to dry outlook until September, with a sudden shift to wet from October, in agreement with the expected influence of ongoing El Niño conditions.

GNB.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

IDN.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

ETH.comment: During July, rainfall deficits in the initial part of the Meher season have worsened with up to 30% below average rainfall in large parts of Northern Ethiopia, Amhara and in the Rift Valley. Also, temperatures in July have been significantly above average with heatwaves reported across the country. ASAP forecasts warnings based on seasonal rainfall forecasts are showing a high risk for these areas of continued below average rainfall throughout the season. This forecast is in line with El Niño conditions worsening during the second half of 2026. Pastoral regions in the country are facing similar risks and whereas rainfall deficits started in July in the southern part of the country, negative impacts of the hot and dry conditions are already visible in pastoral areas in the Afar, Tigray and Shewa zones. In the just concluded Belg 2026 season, agroclimatic conditions have generally been favourable, with an early onset of rainfall and cumulative precipitation close to the seasonal average across most cropping areas. Despite the favourable Belg season conditions, concerns over the food security outlook situation are rapidly increasing, driven by the negative early Meher season conditions and by rapidly increasing food and fuel prices during the lean season, which continue to erode household purchasing power. While the Belg harvest is expected to provide some improvement in local food availability, its contribution to the overall food supply is modest, as the Belg season accounts for less than 10% of Ethiopia's annual cereal production and is therefore unlikely to substantially ease current food security pressures.

KAZ.comment: In southern Kazakhstan, harvest of winter wheat (which represents 5% of the total wheat production) is underway and crop biomass suggests a close to average output. In the main producing regions of the north (Severo, Kustanayskaia and Akmolinskaya), spring wheat and barley (which account for 95% of cereals output) are in vegetative to reproductive stage with well above average biomass thanks to favourable rainfall and above average temperature conditions. Prospects for spring wheat and barley, to be harvested from August to October, are therefore very good.

THA.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

NPL.comment: In Nepal, rice planting is underway (see for instance [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/9ac223c1] S2 image of Central in July and June 2026) under favourable rainfall conditions while maize is approaching harvest under favourable moisture conditions.

COL.comment: In July, all major crops are in harvest stage. Maize and paddy output in 2026 anticipated below average due to low plantings ([https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/giews-country-brief-colombia-21-july-2026] GIEWS). Cumulative rainfall of the past three months has been below average with poor vegetation conditions shown across cropping areas, particularly in the rice-producing areas of Tolima and Huila, where over 43% and 37% of their respective agricultural active areas exhibit poor vegetation health. According to the ([https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel), there is a very high probability that conditions will be drier than normal in the northern and western part of the country due to the rapid transition to a strong El Niño pattern heading into the second half of 2026 ([https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-forecast-intensify-increasing-likelihood-of-extreme-weather] WMO).

GIN.comment: Planting of coarse grain crops (maize, millet, and sorghum) was completed in June, while planting operations for rice, the most important crop produced in the country, will conclude in August. As of mid-July, crop and rangeland conditions are good across the country, except for the eastern regions of Kankan and Nzérékoré, where approximately 30% to 35% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the August–September 2026 period points to average rainfall conditions across the country, except for the western part where drier-than-average conditions are forecast.

BEN.comment: Across the southern and central bimodal areas of Benin, cumulative rainfall from the start of the rainy season in March until mid-July has been close to average, benefiting crop and rangeland conditions. Harvesting operations in the south are expected to begin in August, with an average output projected. Conversely, in the northern unimodal areas, where the planting of coarse grain and rice crops was finalized in July, cumulative rainfall over the past month was ca.30% to 40% below average. As a result, crop and rangeland conditions are well below average across the northern provinces of Alibori, Borgou, Atakora, and Donga, where negative greenness anomalies currently affect 50% to 70% of the active crop area and 30% to 60% of the active rangeland area. Persistent insecurity appears to be a key driver of the poor crop conditions observed in these northern regions. As reported by [https://reliefweb.int/report/benin/wfp-benin-country-brief-july-2026] WFP (Benin Country Brief, July 2026), escalating violence linked to the Sahel crisis is expanding from northern into central Benin, driving displacement, increasing protection risks, and creating severe humanitarian access constraints in previously stable zones like Borgou and Donga. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast  for the August–September 2026 period points to average rainfall conditions across the country.

GNQ.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

PAK.comment: In Pakistan, sowings of kharif maize and rice finalized with sufficient irrigation water as the main dams (Tarbela and Mangla) are filled at 72% of their capacity (according to [https://www.facebook.com/ItsTrendingPakistan/posts/pakistans-major-dams-have-reached-72-of-their-combined-storage-capacity-offering/1358096646449813/] Trending Pakistan) thanks to good rainfall received in the first part of the year. Despite low rainfall in the last month in the south (Sindh received only 20% of its usual rainfall), rice fields were flooded as in 2025 (see [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/eba6e24e] S2 imagery of Sindh in July and June 2026). As a result, biomass of kharif crops (rice, maize, millet but also cotton and sugar cane) is now close to (Sindh, Balochistan) or above (Punjab) average. However rainfall is forecast below average for the remaining monsoon months (August and September), which might reduce irrigation water availability.

PER.comment: In July, all major food crops are in the harvesting stage except potato, which normally remains in the vegetation stage until mid-August. Rainfall in the last 30 days has been normal in most cropping areas but below average in the north and northeastern part of the country. In particular, large areas of San Martin (34%) and Amazonas (27%), both key rice-producing departments, are experiencing poor vegetation conditions, also driven by a reduction in sown cereal areas ([https://cdn.www.gob.pe/uploads/document/file/7825982/6602539-reporte-alertivo-de-avance-de-siembras-mar-2025.pdf?v=1742920259] Government of Perù). According to the ([https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel), there is a very high probability that conditions will be wetter than normal in the coastal areas and normal to drier than normal in the central and western part of the country through the end of the year. In July, the Comisión Multisectorial encargada del Estudio Nacional del Fenómeno "El Niño" maintains a active "Alerta de El Niño Costero" ([https://enfen.imarpe.gob.pe/] ENFEN).

UGA.comment: The first cropping season has ended across the bimodal areas of central and southern Uganda, with mixed production outcomes expected. Agro-climatic conditions were generally favourable during the onset of the season from February through March, supporting timely planting and good crop establishment. However, the uneven distribution of rainfall during April, May, and June, followed by prolonged dry spells in several areas, likely constrained crop development during the critical stages. IPC estimates for the current period (April – July 2026) In Karamoja region show that 473,000 people are in IPC Phase 3 or above) including 41,000 people in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) and 432,000 in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis).

SWZ.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country, and the cereal output is expected to be above the five-year average ([https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] FAO, Crop Prospects and Food Situation (July 2026)). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

TCD.comment: The 2026 cropping season for maize, millet, sorghum, and rice has gradually advanced northward. Although rainfall conditions have improved since the beginning of June, severe rainfall deficits and high temperatures in May caused widespread moisture stress and delayed vegetation development across major agricultural zones. As of mid-July, both cropland and rangeland biomass conditions remain below-average across most parts of the country. At the national level, more than 50% of the active crop area and close to 40% of the active rangeland area are affected by a negative greenness anomaly. Severe food insecurity will persist across eastern and western Chad through January 2027, driven by livelihoods lost to conflict, high food prices, and a delayed rainy season that are forcing refugees, returnees, and internally displaced persons into Crisis (IPC Phase 3 and 3!) conditions ([https://fews.net/west-africa/chad/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWSNET, June 2026). Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 points to drier-than-average conditions across all agricultural areas of Chad.

ZWE.comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country. Zimbabwe's Second Round of the Crop, Livestock, and Fisheries Assessment (CLAFA 2) report projects a 2% rise in maize output to 2.35 million tonnes for the 2025/2026 season, with total cereal production reaching 2.74 million tonnes ([https://www.veritaszim.net/node/7944" target="_blank] Post-Cabinet Press Briefing (Veritas Zimbabwe). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

BFA.comment: Sowing of sorghum and millet is ongoing and will be finalized by the end of July, while maize is already in the growing stage. Over the past month, a significant portion of central, northern, and eastern Burkina Faso experienced cumulative rainfall deficits. As a result, below-average vegetation conditions are now visible across the central, western, northern, and southeastern parts of the country. Specifically, the central regions of Centre-ouest, Plateau Central, and Centre show poor crop biomass across 30% to 55% of their active cropland. A similar trend appears in the west (Hauts-bassins), north (Nord), and southeast (Centre-est), where approximately 30% of the active crop area is experiencing poor biomass development. While it is still early in the season and conditions require close monitoring over the coming weeks, pastoral conditions in mid-July remain generally good across the country, except for slightly below-average conditions in central areas. Looking ahead, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_07_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for August–September 2026 points to drier-than-average conditions across most of the country, with average rainfall expected only in the southeastern and northeastern border regions.

SYR.comment: In Syria, harvest of winter wheat and barley finalized in all areas, including the northwestern governorates where cereals growth was delayed by 1 to 2 months (Aleppo, Idleb, Hama, Homs) due to rainfall deficit at the start of season, particularly in November. As from December, rainfall conditions improved, causing even flooding in the north. As a result, crop biomass is well above average in all governorates and output prospects are very favourable, in strong contrast with previous year. Food insecurity remains high with about 6 million people in need of food assistance (for a total population of 24 million) according to [https://fews.net/middle-east-and-europe/syria/food-security-outlook/june-2026/print] FEWSNET June report, mainly as a result of the economic situation, which affects especially poor households and IDPs (despite favourable weather conditions) and reduction in humanitarian assistance in 2026.
